newsitem.title: USA: UAW strikes GM Mich. plant after talks break off.
newsitem.headline: UAW strikes GM Mich. plant after talks break off.

text.p: One week after settling the longest strike against General Motors Corp. in decades, United Auto Workers union members walked off the job at a key GM engine component plant at midnight on Tuesday.

The latest walkout came when bargainers failed to produce a new contract by an 11:59 p.m. EDT Tuesday deadline. The strike at GM's Warren, Michigan, tranmission plant affects about 2,800 hourly workers from UAW Local 909.

Early Wednesday, talks continued at a GM Delphi Interior & Lighting plant in Anderson, Indiana, after the UAW extended the 12:59 a.m. EDT (0459 GMT) deadline, said Fred Haney, a spokesman for Local 663.
A strike at either plant could quickly disrupt GM's North American production. Two strikes during the second quarter have already cost the No. 1 U.S. automaker $490 million in lost profits.

The Warren factory produces four-speed automatic transmissions for cars and light trucks, including GM's brisk-selling minivans. The Anderson plant has about 2,500 workers who produce tail lamps and brake lights for nearly all of GM's North American vehicles.

Pickets went up outside the Warren facility shortly after the deadline expired. Local 909 Financial Secretary Jim Marcum said he did not want to strike the automaker, but added, "When it's time to go, it's time to go."
GM spokeswoman Christine D'Angela said both sides were scheduled to meet again at 9 a.m. EDT (1300 GMT) Wednesday.
"They were working real hard, but when the midnight hour came they had not reached an agreement," she said.

Last Friday, 5,850 workers from UAW Local 594 approved a settlement reached on July 16 with GM. The pact ended an 87-day strike at the Pontiac, Michigan, full-size pickup truck plant. It was the longest walkout at GM in more than 25 years.
As part of the new accord, GM agreed to add 557 new production and skilled trades workers and pay a total of $9.5 million to settle grievances and cover missed holiday pay.

The Warren and Anderson strike deadlines were the most recent skirmishes between GM and the UAW. Union resistance to GM's efforts to cut its workforce and send more work to outside contractors has lead to a rancorous year of labour negotiations, including five strikes and numerous strike deadlines.

GM says it requires fewer workers to produce its newest generation of vehicles, and needs to slash overall manufacturing costs to stay competitive. Union leaders insist GM add more staffing to reduce overtime burdens and improve health and safety. The union also wants to bolster job security by forcing GM to limit how much work it sends to outside contractors.

A new national contract between GM and the UAW was signed last November. But the conflicts over staffing and outsourcing has lead to slow bargaining progress. Of GM's 105 UAW locals, about 10 still do not have new contracts.
By contrast, the other members of Detroit's Big Three, Ford Motor Co. and Chrysler Corp., had their local contracts wrapped up months ago.
